strengths: The paper identifies a useful issue in multi-agent curricula: increasing agent count can make reward acquisition easier while changing coordination difficulty. This motivates adapting agent counts instead of assuming that fewer agents always provide easier training tasks.

Combining self-paced RL with agent-count contexts and an existing critic-loss signal is a simple, potentially useful practical contribution. Parameter sharing and observation padding provide a plausible implementation path.

The three sparse-reward settings provide encouraging evidence for adaptive curricula: SPRL and SPMARL learn where target-only MAPPO fails. Simple-Spread and SMACv2 also show an early learning advantage for SPMARL over SPRL.

Reporting target-task performance separately from training returns and plotting the generated curricula makes the results informative. The Simple-Spread experiment specifies five seeds and 95% confidence intervals, and the manuscript provides a code link.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of critic loss as learning progress is not established. Equation (8) measures prediction error: conditional on a state, expected squared return error equals return variance plus squared value-estimation bias. It can therefore remain high for a fixed policy with an accurate critic, particularly in stochastic environments. Conversely, zero-return tasks can yield zero loss without useful learning. CTDE does not eliminate these problems. No diagnostic connects the proposed score to subsequent policy improvement or improved credit assignment, leaving the principal mechanistic claims unsupported.

The novelty discussion omits closely related prediction-error-based curricula, particularly Prioritized Level Replay (Jiang et al., ICML 2021), which uses value-error signals to prioritize training levels. Applying such signals within SPRL to agent-count curricula may still be useful, but the claimed novelty needs clearer positioning. SPRL alone also does not adequately represent methods that prioritize improvements in return rather than high returns.

The baseline comparisons do not convincingly establish superiority over existing multi-agent curriculum approaches. A linear schedule does not reproduce the additional mechanisms in FewToMore, EPC, or VACL. In Simple-Spread, the chosen fewer-to-more schedule follows the direction that the paper itself explains is ineffective. A tuned decreasing or performance-triggered schedule would be a more informative comparison, alongside a competing learning-progress curriculum.

Evidence for the incremental benefit of SPMARL is limited. SPRL and SPMARL attain similar final performance, and their XOR evaluation curves nearly coincide. The convergence-speed claim needs quantitative sample-efficiency summaries with uncertainty; the seed and confidence-interval protocol is explicit only for Simple-Spread. There are no ablations or sensitivity studies establishing robustness to the performance threshold, context initialization, or critic fitting, despite their direct influence on the proposed mechanism.

The optimization is not well defined as written. Equation (6) minimizes KL(p || mu), while mu is described as a Dirac target and p as Gaussian; this divergence is infinite for a nondegenerate Gaussian. Any target smoothing or alternative implemented objective must be specified. There is also a control-flow discrepancy: Section 4.1 describes freezing the curriculum when performance drops below threshold after entering stage two, whereas Algorithm 1 returns to the learning-progress update.

The manuscript leaves substantial reproduction details to the linked code, including network and optimization settings, complete context bounds and initial distributions, task-specific thresholds and KL bounds, and critic-loss normalization and timing. The XOR setup also needs an explanation of how shared policies distinguish agents and accommodate changing action spaces. These omissions hinder assessment of the modified benchmarks and comparisons. A separate minor correction is that Section 5.3 states a target of eight agents although the task and Figure 7 specify five.
